title: Tehanu
author: Le Guin, Ursula K.
review:
Honestly not sure what to rate this, don't take my rating too seriously

Definitely glad I read the book even though it was sort of a bleak tough read with a lot of anger and fear towards how our society (and the society of Earthsea) is structured and the power imbalances that arise from this structure.

After the previous books being epic and mythological this book is very grounded and mundane, it's also the darkest one yet and there's quite a lot of "sociological horror" surrounding what it's like to be a woman, child, or the poor in this society and how grim the prospects really are in these circumstances.

However there's still moments of beauty and light. I did find this as an interesting meditation on what it's like to be past your prime and aging and thinking about what happens when you feel inadequate and fixating on past failures.

Le Guin really gives me a lot to think about and I think I'll sit on this one for a while and digest it a bit before continuing to her short stories but I always find something in her works to ponder deeply. She definitely has a lot of wisdom and has some great ideas about a large swath of themes and topics.

This sort of feels like a sister novel to Left Hand of Darkness even though I haven't read it, but makes me more interested in what she has to say about gender in her other works.

highlights.text: I used to live in a silent house, alone, she thought. I will do so again.
He opened his eyes and gazed through a gap in the thickets at the western sky. He seemed to watch something, some act or deed, in that far, clear, golden space of light.
There was nothing she could do, but there was always the next thing to be done.

Somebody in this fine household—a witch, a widow, a cripple, and a half-wit—had to do what must be done, and not frighten the child with weeping. But the dragon was gone, and was there nothing to come anymore but death?
“Well, well,” the older woman said; and after a while, “Dearie, there’s misery enough without going looking for it.”
“Coming back from death must be a long journey—even on the dragon’s back. It will take time. Time and quiet, silence, stillness. You have been hurt. You will be healed.”
And so we must live on into the new age with the spoils of our victory over evil. You with your burned child, and I with nothing at all.” Despair speaks evenly, in a quiet voice.

Who are we? What is it to be a man? Before he had his name, before he had knowledge, before he had power, the hawk was in him, and the man, and the mage, and more—he was what we cannot name. And so are we all.”
“What I don’t understand is why he brought me back. The kindness of the young is cruelty…. So I’m here, I have to get on with it, till I can go back.”
But even so she did not feel she understood his shame, his agony of humiliation. Perhaps only a man could feel so. A woman got used to shame.
“You’ll know the value of a good reputation,” Moss said dryly, “when you’ve lost it.
To be a woman was her fault. Nothing could worsen or amend it, in his eyes; no punishment was enough. He had looked at what had been done to Therru, and approved.

We died together. Together we crossed the mountains there. You can come back across the mountains. There is a way. He knew it. But the name of the mountains is Pain. The stones… The stones cut, and the cuts are long to heal.”
“Lady Tenar, you say you fled from one enemy and found another; but I came seeking a friend, and found another.”
He thought he had learned pain, but he would learn it again and again, all his life, and forget none of it.
He would turn as the trumpets sounded and seat himself on the throne that had been empty so many years, and look at his kingdom with those dark eyes that knew what pain was, what fear was.
Both manhood and magery are built on one rock: power belongs to men. If women had power, what would men be but women who can’t bear children? And what would women be but men who can?”
